Discourse on Ignorance:
Is there ignorance in an arahant?
Yes, [you say].

Is there, for an Arahant, ignorance, the flood of ignorance, the yoke of ignorance, the underlying tendency to ignorance, the obsession of ignorance, the fetter of ignorance, and the hindrance of ignorance?
One should not say so.

Is it not the case that there is no ignorance, no flood of ignorance, no yoke of ignorance, no underlying tendency to ignorance, no obsession of ignorance, no fetter of ignorance, and no hindrance of ignorance for an Arahant?
“Yes.

“If there is no ignorance in an Arahant—no flood of ignorance, no yoke of ignorance, no underlying tendency to ignorance, no obsession by ignorance, no fetter of ignorance, and no hindrance of ignorance—then indeed, sir, you should not say:
‘An Arahant possesses non-knowing.’”

There is ignorance in an ordinary person; there is in him the flood of ignorance, the yoke of ignorance, the underlying tendency to ignorance, the obsession of ignorance, the fetter of ignorance, and the hindrance of ignorance—is this so?
Yes.

Is there ignorance in an Arahant; is there in him the flood of ignorance, the yoke of ignorance, the underlying tendency to ignorance, the obsession of ignorance, the fetter of ignorance, and the hindrance of ignorance—is this so?
It should not be said so.

Is it the case that while an Arahant has ignorance (aññāṇa), he does not have ignorance (avijjā), the flood of ignorance, the yoke of ignorance, the underlying tendency to ignorance, the obsession of ignorance, the fetter of ignorance, or the hindrance of ignorance?
Yes, it is.

Is there ignorance in an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), but no "flood of ignorance," "yoke of ignorance," "underlying tendency of ignorance," "obsession of ignorance," "fetter of ignorance," or "hindrance of ignorance" for him?
One should not say so. Is there non-knowing in an Arhat? One should not say so.
“Yes. “An arahant, being prompted by ignorance, might kill a living being, take what is not given, speak falsehood,
speak maliciously, speak harshly, engage in idle chatter, break into a dwelling, carry off plunder, or commit burglary.”

Would he do so? Would he stand in ambush? Would he go to another's wife? Would he commit the destruction of a village? Would he commit the destruction of a town? Certainly not; such should not be said.

Yet there is ignorance in the worldling (*puthujjana*); being overcome by ignorance, does the worldling kill a living being, take what is not given, speak falsehood... [and so on] ...would he commit the destruction of a village? Would he commit the destruction of a town? [Yes, he would.]
“Yes,” you say.

“Then does an Arahant have ignorance? Could an Arahant, being characterized by ignorance, kill a living being, take what is not given, [and so forth] … commit the destruction of a village, or commit the destruction of a town?
You must not say so.

"There is ignorance in an Arahant, yet an Arahant would not, impelled by ignorance, kill a living being, take what is not given, [and so on] … commit the destruction of a village, or commit the destruction of a town."— Yes.

"There is ignorance in an ordinary person (puthujjana), yet an ordinary person would not, impelled by ignorance, kill a living being, take what is not given, [and so on] … commit the destruction of a village, or commit the destruction of a town"?— [No.]
It should not be said so.
Is there ignorance in an Arahant? Yes.
"Is there, for an Arahant, ignorance regarding the Teacher, ignorance regarding the Dhamma, ignorance regarding the Saṅgha,

ignorance regarding the training, ignorance regarding the past, ignorance regarding the future, ignorance regarding both the past and the future, and ignorance regarding specific conditionality and dependently arisen phenomena?
"One should certainly not say so."
"Is it not the case that for an Arahant there is no ignorance regarding the Teacher, no ignorance regarding the Dhamma, no ignorance regarding the Saṅgha, no ignorance regarding the training,

no ignorance regarding the past, no ignorance regarding the future, no ignorance regarding both the past and the future, and no ignorance regarding specific conditionality and dependently arisen phenomena? "Yes, it is."

If there is no ignorance regarding the Teacher, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha …pe… and regarding phenomena that have arisen through specific conditionality and dependent origination in an Arahant, then surely you should not say, "There is ignorance in an Arahant.

Is there ignorance in an ordinary person (puthujjana)? Is there ignorance regarding the Teacher, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha …pe… and regarding phenomena that have arisen through specific conditionality and dependent origination in him?
“Yes,” [you say].

“Then there is ignorance in the Arahant; there is his ignorance regarding the Teacher, ignorance regarding the Dhamma, ignorance regarding the Saṅgha …pe… ignorance regarding the specific conditionality and dependently arisen phenomena?
You should not speak thus.

"There is ignorance in an Arahant; yet there is no ignorance in him regarding the Teacher, no ignorance regarding the Dhamma, no ignorance regarding the Saṅgha …pe… no ignorance regarding phenomena that have arisen through specific conditionality and dependent origination"?
"Yes.

"There is ignorance in an ordinary person (puthujjana); yet there is no ignorance in him regarding the Teacher, no ignorance regarding the Dhamma, no ignorance regarding the Saṅgha …pe… no ignorance regarding phenomena that have arisen through specific conditionality and dependent origination"? [Is this the case?]
It should not be said so.
Is there ignorance in an Arahant? Yes.
Is it not the case that for an Arahant, lust is abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and subject to non-arising in the future?
Yes, it is.

If for an Arahant lust is abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and subject to non-arising in the future, then indeed, you should not say: [that he still possesses lust].
“There is ignorance in an Arahant.
Is there ignorance in an Arahant? Yes.
Is it not the case that for an Arahant, hatred has been abandoned … pe … delusion has been abandoned … pe … and moral shamelessness has been abandoned,
cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and subject to non-arising in the future?
“Yes.

“If, for an Arahant, fearlessness of wrongdoing has been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and is of a nature not to arise again in the future, then surely it should not be said:
‘There is ignorance in an Arahant.’”

"Are the factors of enlightenment developed? "Yes.
"If the factors of enlightenment are developed for the abandoning of lust in an Arahant, then indeed, sir, you should not say—"
“There is ignorance in the Arahant.
Is there ignorance in the Arahant?
Yes, [you say].
Is it not the case that for an Arahant,
the path has been cultivated for the abandoning of hatred … pe … for the abandoning of delusion … pe … for the abandoning of moral fearlessness? … pe …
"Are the factors of enlightenment developed for the abandoning of non-fearlessness in an Arahant? "Yes.
"If the factors of enlightenment are indeed developed by an Arahant for the abandoning of non-fearlessness, then, alas, you should certainly not say—"
“There is ignorance in the Arahant.
Is there ignorance in the Arahant? Yes.
Is it not the case that the Arahant is one who is free from lust, free from hatred,
and free from delusion … [as before] … and has realized what ought to be realized?
Yes, it is.
If an arahant is one who is free from lust … [and so on] … and has realized what is to be realized, then indeed, it should not be said:
“There is ignorance in an arahant.”
Is there ignorance in an Arahant?
There is ignorance in an Arahant who is skilled in his own doctrine, but there is no ignorance in an Arahant who is skilled in another’s doctrine.
Is there ignorance in an Arahant who is skilled in his own doctrine?
“Yes,” [you say].
“Then does an Arahant who is skilled in others’ doctrines possess ignorance?
You should not say so … [and so on] …
Is it not the case that for an arahant skilled in the supreme dhamma there is no ignorance?
Yes, it is so.
Is it not the case that for an arahant skilled in his own dhamma there is no ignorance? Yes, it is so.
It should not be said thus… [as before]… Is it the case that for an Arahant skilled in his own doctrine, lust has been abandoned, yet ignorance still exists in him? Yes.
Is it not to be said that for an Arahant skilled in the supreme Dhamma, lust has been abandoned, yet ignorance still exists?
One should certainly not say so …pe….
For an Arahant skilled in his own Dhamma, hatred has been abandoned …pe….
Delusion has been abandoned … [and so on] … fearlessness of wrongdoing has been abandoned; does he still possess ignorance? Yes.
Is it not the case that for an Arahant skilled in the supreme Dhamma, shamelessness has been abandoned, yet there still exists ignorance in him?
One should not say so …pe….
For an Arahant skilled in his own Dhamma, the path has been cultivated for the abandoning of lust …pe….
If you say "yes"— that the factors of enlightenment have been developed, yet there is still ignorance in him—
then does it follow that for an Arahant skilled in the qualities of others, who has developed the factors of enlightenment for the abandoning of lust, there is still ignorance in him?
It should not be stated thus … [as before] … for the sake of an Arahant skilled in his own Dhamma to abandon hatred … [as before] … to abandon delusion … [as before].
If the path has been developed for the abandoning of lack of moral dread … and the factors of enlightenment have been developed, is there still ignorance in him? Yes.
The factors of enlightenment have been developed by the Arahant skilled in the supreme Dhamma for the abandoning of fearlessness; does it follow that there is ignorance in him?
One should not say so …pe….
The Arahant skilled in his own Dhamma is free from lust, free from hatred, and free from delusion …pe….
Is there ignorance regarding that which is to be realized as having been realized?
Yes. Is an Arahant—one skilled in the qualities of others, free from lust, free from hatred, and free from delusion … [as before] … ignorant of this? Yes.
That which is to be realized has been realized; is there, then, ignorance regarding it?
One should not say so... [and so on].
For an Arahant skilled in the qualities of others, lust has been abandoned; is there, then, no ignorance regarding that?
“Yes,” [you say].
“Is lust abandoned by an Arahant who is skilled in the True Dhamma, yet there is no ignorance in him?
You should not speak thus … [and so on] … .
Has hatred been abandoned by the Arahant who is supremely skilled; ...
has delusion been abandoned; ...
has lack of moral dread been abandoned? Is there no ignorance remaining for him?
“Yes.
“Then, for an Arahant skilled in the True Dhamma, has fearlessness been abandoned, yet there is no ignorance in him?
“You should not say so…” [and so on].

For the Arahant, who is supremely skilled, the path has been developed for the abandoning of lust …pe… the factors of enlightenment have been developed …pe… for the abandoning of hatred and for the abandoning of delusion …pe…
Is it not the case that for one who has cultivated the path for the abandoning of lack of moral dread,
and likewise cultivated the factors of enlightenment, there is no ignorance?
Yes, it is so.
Is it not the case that for an Arahant skilled in his own Dhamma, the factors of enlightenment have been developed for the abandoning of fearlessness,
and thus there is no ignorance in him?
One should not say so … [as before] … An Arahant skilled in the Dhamma of others is free from lust, free from hatred, and free from delusion … [as before].
Is that which is to be realized already realized, such that there is no ignorance regarding it? Yes.
Is an Arahant—one skilled in his own Dhamma, free from lust, free from hatred, and free from delusion … [and so forth] … [ignorant]? No.
"Is that which is to be realized already realized, such that there is no ignorance regarding it?
"One should not say so...
[and so on] "...Is there ignorance in the Arahant?"
“Yes, [it is so].
“Has it not been said by the Blessed One:
‘Monks, I declare the destruction of the taints for one who knows and sees, not for one who does not know and does not see’?”
And what, bhikkhus, is it that one who knows and sees thus experiences the destruction of the taints?
"Such is form, such its origin, such its passing away; such is feeling … such is perception …" [and so on].
“‘Such is volitional formations...
such is consciousness, such its origin, such its passing away.
It is for one who knows thus and sees thus, monks, that the destruction of the taints occurs.”
Is it indeed a sutta? Yes.
Therefore, it should not be said—
“There is ignorance in the Arahant.
Is there ignorance in the Arahant? Yes.
Has it not been said by the Blessed One:
“Bhikkhus, I declare that the destruction of the taints occurs for one who knows and sees, not for one who does not know and does not see.
And what, bhikkhus, is it that one must know and see for the destruction of the taints to occur?”
“‘This is suffering’—for one who knows and sees this, monks, there is the destruction of the taints.
‘This is the origin of suffering’—for one who knows and sees this, there is the destruction of the taints. ‘This is the cessation of suffering’—”

For one who knows and sees, there is the destruction of the taints: “This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering”—for one who knows and sees this, there is the destruction of the taints.
It is in this way, monks, that for one who knows and sees, there is the destruction of the taints.
Is it indeed a sutta? Yes.
Therefore, it should not be said—
“There is ignorance in the Arahant.
Is there ignorance in the Arahant? Yes.
But has it not been said by the Blessed One:

“Bhikkhus, without directly knowing and fully understanding everything, without becoming dispassionate toward it and abandoning it, one is incapable of the destruction of suffering; but, bhikkhus, by directly knowing and fully understanding everything, by becoming dispassionate toward it and abandoning it, one is capable of the destruction of suffering”?
Is this indeed the Suttanta?
“Yes, [it is so].
Therefore, it should not be said:
“There is ignorance in the Arahant.”
"Is there ignorance in an Arahant?
"Yes.
"But has it not been said by the Blessed One:"
“With the attainment of vision,
three things are abandoned by him:
personality-belief, doubt, and
Whatever rules and observances there may be,
he is utterly freed from the four states of misery and incapable of committing the six acts of immediate retribution.
Is it indeed a sutta? Yes.
Therefore, it should not be said—
“There is ignorance in the Arahant.
Is there ignorance in the Arahant? Yes.
Has it not been said by the Blessed One:
“Bhikkhus, at whatever time the dustless, stainless Dhamma-eye arises in a noble disciple—
‘Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease’— with the arising of that vision, bhikkhus, three fetters are abandoned in the noble disciple:”
“Personality-belief, doubt, and adherence to rules and observances.
Is this indeed a sutta?
Yes, it is.
Therefore, it should not be said:
"There is ignorance in the Arahant.
It should not be said.
“Does an Arahant have ignorance?”—
“Yes.”—
“But would an Arahant not fail to know the names and clans of men and women, fail to know what is the path and what is not the path, and fail to know the names of grasses, sticks, and forest trees?”
“Yes.

“If an Arahant did not know the names and clans of men and women, did not know what is the path and what is not the path, and did not know the names of grasses, sticks, and forest trees, then indeed, sir,
you must admit that there is ignorance in an Arahant.”

"An Arahant would not know the names and clans of men and women; he would not know what is the path and what is not the path; he would not know the names of grasses, wood, and forest trees—thus, does an Arahant possess ignorance?
"Yes.
"Then an Arahant would not know the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning, or even Arahantship?"
It should not be stated thus... [etc.
...The discussion on ignorance is finished.
